code.title: Race condition without a data race: check-then-act

followUps:
Yes: two threads each check a balance under a lock and then withdraw under a second lock. Every access is locked, so there is no data race, but the check can be stale by the time of the act.

Example: balance 100, both threads see 100 >= 80, both subtract 80, final -60. The program shows this. Fix it by holding one lock across check and act, or by using a single compare-exchange.

ThreadSanitizer records, for every memory access, which thread touched it and that thread's logical clock (a vector clock), then reports two conflicting accesses that have no happens-before relation between them.

The compiler (-fsanitize=thread) inserts a call before each load and store, and mutex and atomic operations update the clocks. Shadow memory keeps the last few accesses per 8 bytes. Cost: roughly 5 to 15 times slower and 5 to 10 times more memory. It only reports races that actually happen in the run you test.

code.title: join() and jthread: joining automatically

followUps:
Because an automatic join could block for a long time, or forever, inside a destructor, which often runs during stack unwinding, and it would hide the cost. Aborting made the bug loud.

The committee considered both choices bad (auto-join may hang, auto-detach leaves dangling references) so it chose the one that can never silently misbehave: std::terminate. std::jthread in C++20 later added auto-join together with a stop request, so the join can actually finish.

Detach is fine when the thread owns everything it uses and nobody needs its result: for example a fire-and-forget task that works only on data it copied or moved in, and where being killed at process exit is harmless.

Never detach a thread that captures locals by reference, uses an object that may be destroyed first, or must finish its work (flush a file). Even then a tracked pool or a jthread is usually safer, since a detached thread cannot be waited for at shutdown.

code.title: lock_guard, unique_lock and scoped_lock

followUps:
It uses a try-and-back-off strategy, so it never waits for one mutex while holding another in a way that can form a cycle.

A typical implementation (libstdc++) locks the first mutex, then try_locks the next ones. If any fails, it unlocks everything it holds and starts again with the failing mutex as the one to lock first. Because a thread holding a lock never blocks for another, the circular-wait condition cannot hold. Cost: it can spin under heavy contention, but the order of arguments no longer matters.

Because the lock is released when the method returns, so the caller then reads or writes the data with no lock held, which is a data race.

int& get() { lock_guard g(m); return v; }
int x = obj.get();   // lock already released
obj.get() = 5;       // unprotected write

Return a copy, or take a callback that runs under the lock (withLocked(f)), or return a small guard object that carries the lock.

code.title: Preventing deadlock with a global lock order

followUps:
Deadlock means threads wait for each other forever; livelock means they keep running and reacting to each other but make no progress; starvation means one thread is never scheduled or never wins the lock, while others progress.

Example: two people in a corridor. Deadlock is both standing still. Livelock is both stepping aside in the same direction again and again. Starvation is one person never getting through because a stream of others always goes first. Fixes: lock order, randomized back-off, and fair locks or queues.

Priority inversion is when a high-priority thread waits for a lock held by a low-priority thread, and a medium-priority thread keeps the low one from running, so the high one is effectively blocked by the medium one.

Example: low L holds a mutex, high H waits for it, medium M runs forever, so L never gets CPU to release. Fix: priority inheritance (L temporarily runs at H's priority), which real-time mutexes such as POSIX PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT provide. This famously hit the Mars Pathfinder.

code.title: condition_variable with a predicate

followUps:
notify_one wakes one waiter; use notify_all when several waiters may need to proceed, or when waiters wait for different conditions on the same condition variable.

Examples: a shutdown flag (every consumer must see it), a barrier that opens for all, or a shared cv with readers and writers waiting for different predicates, where notify_one may wake the wrong one and the signal is wasted. When in doubt use notify_all: waiters re-check their predicate, so the worst case is some extra wakeups.

It is allowed and always correct, but it is usually better to notify after releasing the lock, so the woken thread can take the mutex immediately instead of waking up and blocking again (the "hurry up and wait" problem).

The exception: if the condition variable could be destroyed right after the waiter sees the state change, you must notify while holding the lock, or the notify touches a destroyed object. Either way, change the state under the mutex.

code.title: Bounded blocking queue with close()

followUps:
It is possible with a fixed-size ring buffer and two atomic indices, because only the producer writes tail and only the consumer writes head.

push: t=tail.load(relaxed); if (t+1)%N==head.load(acquire) return false;
      buf[t]=v; tail.store((t+1)%N, release);
pop:  h=head.load(relaxed); if (h==tail.load(acquire)) return false;
      v=buf[h]; head.store((h+1)%N, release);

The release store publishes the slot, the acquire load sees it. One slot stays empty to tell full from empty. No locks, O(1) per operation.

Use wait_for (or wait_until) with the same predicate, and return false or nullopt if it times out.

unique_lock lk(m);
if (!notEmpty.wait_for(lk, 50ms, [&]{ return !d.empty() || closed; }))
    return nullopt;           // timed out
if (d.empty()) return nullopt; // closed
// pop and notFull.notify_one()

The predicate form handles spurious wakeups and recomputes the remaining time for you. Use a steady clock, not the system clock.

code.title: atomic counter vs mutex-guarded invariant

followUps:
False sharing is when two threads write different variables that sit on the same cache line (usually 64 bytes), so the line bounces between cores and both threads slow down even though they share no data.

Example: four counters in an array of long updated by four threads can run several times slower than one counter per thread. Fix: align or pad each hot variable to its own line, struct alignas(64) Slot { long n; };, or use per-thread counters and add them at the end.

No. Lock-free means some thread always makes progress, not that it is faster. Under heavy contention, many CAS retries and cache-line bouncing can be slower than a mutex.

Example: 16 threads hammering one atomic counter can lose to sharded counters (each thread its own, summed at the end). Lock-free also costs complexity (ABA, memory reclamation). Its real benefits are no blocking, no priority inversion and no deadlock. Measure first.

code.title: CAS loop: lock-free atomic max

followUps:
ABA is when a CAS succeeds because a value looks unchanged (A), although it changed to B and back to A in between, so the structure may have changed underneath.

Example: a lock-free stack pops node A (next = B), another thread pops A and B and pushes A back; the first thread's CAS head: A to B succeeds, but B is gone. Fixes: a tagged pointer (pointer plus a version counter, compare both with a double-width CAS, so A with version 1 differs from A with version 3), or hazard pointers or epoch reclamation, which stop A being freed and reused while in use.

A CAS loop is lock-free but not wait-free.

Lock-free: at any moment, at least one thread succeeds, because a CAS only fails when another thread's CAS succeeded. Wait-free would need every thread to finish in a bounded number of steps, but one unlucky thread can keep losing and retrying forever. A single fetch_add on hardware that supports it directly (x86 lock xadd) is wait-free, which is why it is preferred over a CAS loop for counters.

code.title: release/acquire publishing data

followUps:
x86 is strongly ordered: ordinary loads and stores already behave like acquire and release, so the hardware hides the missing ordering. ARM and POWER may reorder most memory operations, so the bug appears there.

Example: data = 42; ready.store(true, relaxed); on x86 the CPU keeps the two stores in order, and the compiler happens not to reorder them. On ARM the reader can see ready == true and data == 0. The code was always wrong in C++; x86 just did not punish it. Test on ARM.

On x86 a seq_cst store compiles to xchg (or mov followed by mfence), while a release store is a plain mov.

The extra cost is the full barrier, which drains the store buffer so the store is globally ordered before later loads. A seq_cst load is just a plain mov. So on x86 the price of seq_cst is paid on stores, usually a few dozen cycles. On ARMv8 both use the dedicated stlr and ldar instructions.

code.title: Happens-before edges between threads

followUps:
A release sequence is a release store followed by later atomic read-modify-writes on the same variable; an acquire load that reads any value in that chain still synchronizes with the first release store.

Example: thread A does x.store(1, release), thread B does x.fetch_add(1, relaxed), thread C does x.load(acquire) and reads 2. C still sees everything A wrote before its release. This is why a reference count with relaxed increments in the middle still works. A plain store by another thread ends the sequence (since C++20).

A release fence before an atomic store, paired with an acquire fence after an atomic load that reads that store, acts like a release store and an acquire load: all writes before the release fence are visible after the acquire fence.

// writer
data = 42;
atomic_thread_fence(memory_order_release);
flag.store(1, relaxed);
// reader
if (flag.load(relaxed) == 1) {
  atomic_thread_fence(memory_order_acquire);  // now data == 42
}

Fences are useful when one fence covers several relaxed operations.

code.title: std::async launch policies and gotchas

followUps:
promise and packaged_task only create the result channel (a future); you decide which thread runs the work. async also starts the work for you.

promise: you call set_value or set_exception yourself. packaged_task: wraps a callable, and running it fills the future; you can move it into a queue or a thread pool. async: picks the thread (or deferred run) and has the blocking-destructor gotcha. Use promise for event-style results, packaged_task for pools, async for quick one-offs.

Keep N worker threads and a queue of packaged_task objects; submit returns the task's future.

auto t = make_shared<packaged_task<R()>>(f);
auto fut = t->get_future();
{ lock_guard g(m); q.push([t]{ (*t)(); }); }
cv.notify_one();
return fut;

Workers pop under the lock and run the job outside it. Exceptions are stored in the future and rethrown by get(). See the working program above.

code.title: A small thread pool with futures

followUps:
Work stealing gives each worker its own deque, so most pushes and pops touch only local memory, and an idle worker steals from the other end of someone else's deque.

Locality: a worker runs the tasks it just created, whose data is still in its cache. Contention: the owner takes from one end (newest), thieves take from the other (oldest, usually the biggest piece of work), so they rarely collide and there is no single hot lock. Compared with one shared queue this scales better beyond about 8 cores.

Never block a pool worker on a future whose task is still in the same pool's queue; instead help run queued tasks while waiting, or use a continuation.

Example: pool of 2 threads, both run tasks that call get() on subtasks that sit behind them in the queue, so no thread is free to run the subtasks: deadlock. Options: make get run other queued tasks while waiting (as work-stealing pools do), use a separate pool for blocking work, give the pool more threads than the nesting depth, or chain with then-style callbacks.

code.title: atomic<shared_ptr> config snapshot

followUps:
The increment only needs atomicity, because nobody uses the count to read the object's data; the decrement must be acq_rel because the thread dropping the last reference then destroys the object.

Thread A writes to the object and drops its reference (release). Thread B drops the last one (acquire), sees A's writes, and destroys the object safely. If the decrement were relaxed, B could run the destructor without seeing A's final writes. An increment from an existing copy is safe because you already hold a reference.

Keep an atomic<shared_ptr<const Config>>. Readers load a snapshot, writers copy, modify and store a whole new object.

auto snap = cfg.load();          // reader: stable view
auto next = make_shared<Config>(*cfg.load());
next->timeout = 30;
cfg.store(next);                 // publish new version

Readers never block and always see a complete, consistent config; the old version is freed when its last reader drops it. With several writers, use compare_exchange so updates are not lost.

code.title: Stress-testing concurrent code

followUps:
Because the printf takes a lock inside the C library and takes time, so it changes the timing and adds ordering between threads, and the race window may close or move.

Output functions use an internal mutex, which gives synchronization edges (happens-before), and the delay can break the unlucky interleaving. Such bugs are called Heisenbugs. The race is still there, so use ThreadSanitizer, which detects the missing happens-before rather than relying on timing.

TSan cannot detect races that do not happen in the run, logic races without a data race, or bugs that need weak-memory orderings it does not model, and it misses some deadlocks.

Details: it only sees executed code paths, so test coverage matters. A check-then-act race on locked data is invisible to it. It does not model all of the relaxed-atomic behaviors of ARM, and fences are handled approximately. It also cannot see code compiled without instrumentation (some libraries) and has a limit on threads and memory. Combine it with stress tests and model checkers.
